q: Why is buying a bigger machine (scaling up) not a lasting answer to big data?
o: Bigger machines cannot run SQL
There is a ceiling on how big one machine gets, and if it crashes everything stops
Bigger machines are slower than small ones
Scaling up requires rewriting the code in Java
e: Scaling up hits the limit of the biggest box you can buy and keeps a single point of failure. Scaling out adds machines and survives the loss of one.

q: What was the key change Apache Spark made compared with Hadoop MapReduce?
o: It stopped distributing data across machines
It replaced SQL with Scala
It keeps intermediate data in memory instead of writing it to disk after every step
It stores data only in a warehouse
e: Spark kept the divide-and-conquer idea but avoided the disk round trip between steps, which made multi-step and iterative jobs much faster.

q: `df.groupBy("city").count()` in PySpark looks like pandas. What is different?
o: Nothing, it runs on the driver like pandas
It only works on CSV files
It needs a Scala compiler
It is executed lazily and in parallel across the machines of the cluster
e: PySpark builds a plan and runs it distributed when an action is called. The syntax is friendly; the execution scales out.

q: Which problem did Delta Lake and the lakehouse solve?
o: Untrusted data lakes on one side and costly warehouse copies on the other
Clusters that were hard to start
Python being slower than Scala
Business users unable to write SQL
e: Delta Lake adds transactions, schema enforcement and history to open files in cheap storage, so one copy of the data serves BI, engineering and AI.

q: A company asks: who can read the salary table, and which dashboards are built on it? Which part of Databricks answers this?
o: Mosaic AI
Unity Catalog
PySpark
Hadoop MapReduce
e: Unity Catalog is the governance layer: permissions, audit logs and lineage for data and AI assets in one place.
